options.label: Runs as the real IR (Recommended)
options.description: The writer produces runs; ANSI is derived from them. This is the architecture originally agreed — sibling encoders off one stream, not one parsing the other. Fixes every finding structurally rather than patching around them, and removes duplication instead of adding it. But it is a substantial rewrite of writer.go's emission path, on the hot path, with byte-identical ANSI across 124 themes as the gate.

options.label: Per-rune capture, measured honestly
options.description: Keep ANSI as the primary output, append per rune into a run buffer behind an off-by-default branch, flush at colour-change events. Smaller and incremental. Costs a predictable branch per rune when off — needs ns/op measurement, not just allocations — and leaves the writer with two parallel notions of output that must agree.

options.label: Pause 2.2 and reassess scope
options.description: The renderer is the largest remaining phase and this is the second time its design has needed rework. Stop, write up what the last two investigations established, and decide whether the SVG encoder is still worth it versus fixing image.go's known defects in place.

input.title: Fix 256-colour blindness in the PNG imager
input.tldr: The PNG exporter can't parse 256-colour escapes, so on terminals without truecolor the images lose all colour and draw escape codes as visible characters.
input.prompt:
In D:\oh-my-posh, `src/cli/image/image.go` builds `ansiSequenceRegexMap` at lines 185-208. It has patterns for truecolor (`\x1b[38;2;r;g;bm` / `48;2;...`) and base-16 (`color16: [349][0-7]|10[0-7]|39`), but **no pattern for 256-colour** (`\x1b[38;5;Nm` / `\x1b[48;5;Nm`).

Those escapes are reachable: `color.TrueColor` is set at `src/terminal/writer.go:258` as `Program != AppleTerminal`, and when false, `color.String.ToAnsi` downgrades hex to 256-colour at `src/color/colors.go:316`. A bare numeric colour string (`"120"`) also always produces 256-colour regardless, at `src/color/colors.go:306-307`.

Consequence: `oh-my-posh config export image` run on Apple Terminal (or with a numeric colour in the config) produces a PNG that loses colour entirely for those segments AND draws the literal escape bytes as visible glyphs, because `processAnsiSequence` returns true (no match) and the loop then renders `\x1b`, `[`, `3`, `8`, `;`, `5`, ... as characters.

Fix: add 256-colour patterns to the regex map and map the palette index to RGB. There is already a base-16 → RGB mapping in `setBase16Color` (`image.go:822+`) to follow for style. The standard xterm 256 palette is: 0-15 the base-16 colours, 16-231 a 6x6x6 RGB cube, 232-255 a 24-step greyscale ramp.

Add a test alongside the existing ones in `src/cli/image/image_test.go` — there are already `processAnsiSequence` tests to model it on.

Verify: `go build ./...` and `go test ./...` clean from `src/`, and `golangci-lint run ./cli/image/...` clean.

input.title: Add TrueColor to the colour cache key
input.tldr: The colour cache ignores whether truecolor is enabled, so changing that setting mid-process serves stale downgraded colours.

In D:\oh-my-posh, `color.Cached.ToAnsi` caches resolved colours keyed on `cachedColorKey{colorString, isBackground}` — see `src/color/colors.go:380-383` and the lookup around `:385-398`.

That key omits `color.TrueColor` (declared `src/color/colors.go:30`, assigned at `src/terminal/writer.go:258` as `Program != AppleTerminal`). But `TrueColor` directly changes the result: `ToAnsi` emits `38;2;r;g;b` when true and downgrades to `38;5;n` when false (`src/color/colors.go:310-317`).

So if `TrueColor` is flipped after any colour has been cached, subsequent lookups return the stale representation. This matters for anything that wants to force truecolor for a non-terminal output target (an image or SVG exporter, for example), and for tests that manipulate it.

The gradient cache already gets this right — `gradientKey` includes `TrueColor` at `src/color/gradient.go:351-353`. Follow that precedent: add the flag to `cachedColorKey` and populate it at the call site.

Note the cache is on by default (`src/config/config.go:90-93`, disabled only by `OMP_CACHE_DISABLED=1`), so this is live behaviour, not a test-only concern.

Add a regression test: resolve a hex colour with `TrueColor` true, flip it to false, resolve the same colour, and assert the second result is the 256-colour form rather than the cached truecolor one.

**Colour resolution must cover every form `Run.BackgroundSource`/`ForegroundSource` can hold**, not just hex:
- `#RRGGBB`
- a colour name from `ansiColorCodes` (`src/color/colors.go:245-263`) — `red`, `lightBlue`, `default`, etc.
- `accent`
- a plain numeric string `0`-`255` (a 256-palette index)
- `transparent`
- **empty** — this is the one that gets missed. `ToAnsi` returns empty on failure (`src/color/colors.go:325`, and `PaletteColors.ToAnsi:359-361` on an unresolved palette key). Nothing is emitted, so the glyph inherits whatever colour was already active. Treat empty as "no colour here, keep the previous" rather than as a colour.

Do NOT resolve colour by parsing `Run.Background`/`Foreground` (the SGR payloads). Those are lossy — the 256-colour downgrade and the sixteen named codes cannot be inverted. That is the failure mode this whole architecture exists to avoid; `src/cli/image/image.go` does it and gets it wrong.

Take the terminal background colour and the accent colour as **explicit inputs** to the encoder rather than reaching for package state, so they can be tested.

**The three `RunMode` values render differently** — read the doc comments in `run.go`. `RunNormal` is the ordinary case. `RunBackgroundPainted` and `RunReverseVideo` are two distinct renderings of transparency; getting them wrong produces invisible or inverted text. Test all three.

**Attributes** are nesting depths, not booleans: `Run.Attributes[i] > 0` means that style is active. Map them to SVG (`font-weight`, `font-style`, `text-decoration`). The slot order matches `knownStyles` in `writer.go` — read it rather than guessing.

## Layout

Monospace cell grid: every cell is one advance wide, `Cells` gives the run's width, so x position is the running cell total. Background is a `<rect>` per run, text is `<text>`. Do not try to measure glyphs — the grid is the point, and it is what makes this correct where the PNG exporter's per-glyph measurement needs a hardcoded double-width table.

Font: reference the family by name (the user has the Nerd Font installed locally). Embedding a subset is a later concern — note it, do not build it.

## Output quality

The SVG must be valid and self-contained, render correctly when opened in a browser, and escape text properly — `&`, `<`, `>` in prompt text must not break the document. Test with text containing all three.

## Verify before reporting

1. `go build ./...`, `go test ./...` clean.
2. **124 goldens still byte-identical** — you should not have touched anything that could move them, so this is a check that you did not.
3. Unit tests for: zero-cell hyperlink runs, all three `RunMode` values, each colour form including empty, attribute mapping, and XML escaping.
4. Actually run it: build the binary, export a real theme to SVG (`themes/jandedobbeleer.omp.json` and `themes/chips.omp.json` are good — chips has a right prompt), and confirm the output parses as XML. Report the byte size versus the equivalent PNG.
5. Open one in a browser if you can, or at minimum verify the structure is sane — correct number of rects, text positioned on the grid, colours matching what the theme specifies.
6. `golangci-lint run ./...` clean.
7. Confirm `git status` shows no changes to `src/terminal/writer.go`.

Report: the package you created and why, the SVG for a small theme (paste it if short), size versus PNG, and anything in the Run stream that turned out to be missing or wrong for this purpose. If some aspect of the rendering cannot be reproduced from the run stream, say so with specifics — that is important information for the next stage, not a failure.

The layout choice is also where SVG structurally beats the PNG path: a monospace cell grid needs no glyph measurement, so it sidesteps the hardcoded double-width table `image.go` maintains by hand — the one whose comment already records a regression from getting powerline separators wrong.

Confirmed: `CGO_ENABLED=0`, `-extldflags "-static"`, cross-compiled for four OSes × three arches from a single job. **resvg can't work here the way you'd want.**

- **CGO binding** — breaks the cross-compile model outright; the project has explicitly committed to static pure-Go builds.
- **WASM via wazero** — technically fine, pure Go, and resvg supports the exact `textLength`/`lengthAdjust` mechanism our SVG depends on. But the only existing Go binding, `kanrichan/resvg-go`, is **GPL-3.0**, and oh-my-posh is MIT distributed through Homebrew, winget and scoop. Statically embedding it would either relicense the binary or isn't permissible. Compiling resvg's own Apache/MIT Rust source to `wasm32-wasi` yourself avoids that, but means owning a Rust→WASM toolchain.
- **oksvg/rasterx** — cannot render `<text>` at all. Our SVG is essentially all text.
- **tdewolff/canvas** — MIT and maintained, but its dependency graph pulls in two GUI toolkits, OpenGL bindings, gonum/plot, a MySQL driver and geo libraries. Deleting 27,700 scoped lines to add that is backwards.

**The realistic alternative** is to keep `gg` but feed it the run stream instead of parsed ANSI. That deletes ~455 of `image.go`'s 920 lines — the entire regex parser, the layout walk, the re-wrapping (redundant, since runs already arrive fit to width), and the hand-maintained double-width table — and kills all four bugs, because `Run` already carries resolved RGB, independent attribute slots, and authoritative cell widths.

But I want to be explicit about the cost, since it differs from what you chose: **it does not delete the 27,700 lines of `gg`/`freetype`/`x-image`.** Those stay.

What does subsetting the font mean?

A font file contains every glyph the font ships — a Nerd Font is on the order of ten thousand, because it merges several icon sets into a normal typeface. That's why the file is megabytes. Any one theme uses almost none of them. Measured earlier on this repo: | | glyphs | |---|---| | all 124 themes combined | 246 | | night-owl (the busiest) | 51 | | a typical theme | a handful | Subsetting means building a new, small font file containing only the glyphs actually used, and dropping the rest. A 51-glyph subset is a few kilobytes instead of a few megabytes. **Why it matters here.** The SVG currently says "draw this in CaskaydiaCove Nerd Font" and relies on the viewer having it installed. Someone browsing the themes gallery to decide whether to try oh-my-posh hasn't installed anything yet, so they'd see tofu boxes where the icons should be — on the exact page meant to sell them the tool. Embedding a subset directly inside the SVG file, as a data URI, removes that dependency. The image carries its own glyphs and renders identically everywhere. It works even in an `` tag because the font is *in* the file — no network fetch, which is the thing that isolation blocks. The cost is bytes. A theme SVG is ~2.6 KB today; a subset would add a few KB. Still an order of magnitude smaller than the 60 KB PNG it replaces, and sharp at any zoom. The catch — and the reason I was mid-investigation when you asked — is that Go has no obvious pure-Go font subsetter. `ConradIrwin/font` is already a dependency but appears to only parse and write whole fonts, not subset them. So the real question is whether this is a small job or a "write a TrueType table serialiser" job, and I'd rather find that out before promising it.
But that does mean that the font could be part of the website, right? That doesn't need to be part of the operating system or anywhere else.
Yes — and that's a better design than what I was heading toward.

Migration running. It's three parts, and the first one is a real finding rather than plumbing.

**The encoder has to change before anything can be inlined.** It emits a bare `text { … }` selector inside a `<style>` block. cd /d/oh-my-posh && git add -A src/ website/ && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
feat(cli)!: export images as SVG only

The image exporter drew its picture by reading back the escape codes the
prompt had already printed. That is why it could not show a theme using
256 colours, could not put bold and italic on the same text, dropped link
targets, and kept a hand-written list of which icons are twice as wide as
the font claims.

Drawing from the prompt's own record of what it rendered removed every one
of those, so the older path had nothing left to offer. It goes, along with
the drawing library, the blur, the font rasteriser and the image package
underneath it: two thousand lines here and four dependencies, and about
nine hundred kilobytes off every binary anyone downloads.

Output is now SVG, which stays sharp at any size and is a fraction of the
bytes.

BREAKING CHANGE: `config export image` writes an SVG and no longer takes
--format, --author, --background-color or --settings. The first has one
option left, and the other three only ever configured the raster canvas:
its caption, its fill, and the sixteen colour codes it substituted. An
existing command line using them now fails rather than quietly producing
something different.

Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
